beats.narration_text: Someone typed the word APPROVE, then hesitated. Wrong verb — Claude doesn't sign your contract. What this skill actually does is narrower and more useful: it reads a folder of contract files, answers your question, and cites exactly where each answer came from. Here's what's happening when you run it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A skill is a folder — three files sitting on disk. Claude opens SKILL.md, reads the instruction set in plain English, then does what it says. No compiled code, no hidden runtime, no proprietary format. They chose text over machinery — you can open it in any editor. The file is the program.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline lives in one section labeled Steps. Claude reads each step in order and runs it. Linear — no branching unless a step says so. That's the design choice: they optimized for auditability over cleverness, so you can trace what ran, in order, every time.

The constraint is deliberately narrow: answer questions across a corpus of contract files, and cite where each answer came from. Everything the skill can do sits inside that one sentence. They optimized for repeatability at the expense of range — it won't argue about a clause; it will show you which paragraph said what, the same way, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read it with me: I have a folder of contract files and a question about them. Read the contracts skill, tell me exactly what you need from me before you run anything, then answer my question across the files and cite where each answer came from. Notice the shape — you're not asking Claude to sign, you're asking it to search and show its work.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It walks the model through what a skill actually is — a folder of plain-text files, no compiled code — and asks it for a concrete example the design fits and one it doesn't. Go deeper: pick a workflow you actually do every week that has three or more repeatable steps. Draft a SKILL.md for it, and see where the design holds up and where it breaks.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how 'skills' work in Claude as a design pattern — folders of plain-text files that Claude reads and executes as instructions, with no compiled code and no hidden runtime. Explain in plain English how a Claude skill differs from a plugin, a library, and an agent. Then give me one concrete example of a task that would be a good candidate for a skill, and one that would not. Sketch what the SKILL.md would contain for the good candidate.
